planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring on free-draining limestone soil; the vine's lanky, curling tendrils and unusually long bunches need sturdy trellising or an old-style pergola.

directions: Girgentina is one of only two grape varieties indigenous to the Maltese islands, likely carried over from Sicily's Agrigento (ancient Girgenti) in antiquity and now listed in Slow Food's Ark of Taste as a heritage crop worth preserving. It yields a light, fresh, low-alcohol white wine and was traditionally also eaten as a table grape or dried, thanks to its notably long, loosely filled clusters. Grow on a pergola or trellis in full sun with sharp drainage, since the variety is prone to mildew in humid, poorly ventilated plantings. Harvest in late summer once the pale green-gold berries soften and sugars rise, before autumn rains can split the thin skins.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in warm, well-drained ground; this dark-skinned vine is Malta's rarer native grape and benefits from a sheltered, wind-protected site.

directions: Ġellewża is Malta's second indigenous grape, a dark-skinned variety grown in far smaller quantities than its companion Girgentina and now threatened by an aging grower base and lengthening droughts. Its thin-skinned berries are pressed into light, medium-bodied reds and strawberry-hued semi-sparkling rosés with bright red-fruit aromas, and winemakers increasingly blend it with Syrah or Cabernet Sauvignon to deepen color and body. Grow on a trellis in a warm, sheltered spot, since the vine is sensitive to strong island winds and benefits from supplemental watering during the driest summer stretches. Pick in early autumn, slightly after Girgentina, once the berries turn deep purple-black.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in alkaline, free-draining soil; some ancient Bidni trees near Bidnija in Malta are protected monuments believed to be over a thousand years old.

directions: Bidni is Malta's own ancient olive cultivar, genetically distinct from mainland Mediterranean types and traditionally grown around the village of Bidnija, where a handful of gnarled, centuries-old trees are now legally protected as national monuments. It bears unusually small, violet-black fruit that is pressed into a notably low-acid, peppery-spicy oil shaped by Malta's alkaline soils, and the same small olives are also cured whole in brine or garlic oil as a table olive. Near-extinction in the twentieth century prompted the 2006 PRIMO revival project, which grafted and distributed roughly 30,000 young Bidni trees to rebuild the orchard base. Grow in full sun on well-drained, lime-rich ground and expect the tree's vigorous, dense habit to need little more than occasional pruning once established.
sources: Malta Ministry for Agriculture, Fisheries and Animal Rights — PRIMO Project

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes into lean, rain-fed soil; this is a late, dryland-adapted variety traditionally grown without irrigation on Mallorca's plains.

directions: Named for the small bunches (ramellets) of about five fruits it sets, this Balearic heirloom from Mallorca, Menorca, and Ibiza was bred for storage rather than fresh eating, with thick skin and a long, slow ripening habit that lets whole clusters be strung up and hung in dry, dim, ventilated rooms for up to nine months without refrigeration. The small, slightly flattened fruit is rarely sliced; instead it is traditionally crushed and rubbed onto bread with olive oil for the classic Mallorcan pa amb oli. Grow on lean, well-drained soil with minimal supplemental water once established, since the variety's dryland hardiness and thick skin are what give it such exceptional keeping power. Spain registered it as a protected conservation variety in 2012 to keep hybridized seed from being sold under the same name.
sources: Conselleria d'Agricultura, Pesca i Medi Natural de les Illes Balears

planting.note: Plant corm offsets after frost danger passes into rich, moisture-retentive ground; the landrace grown around Sotira in Cyprus carries protected EU geographical-indication status.

directions: Known locally as kolokasi, this corm crop grown around the village of Sotira in southeastern Cyprus is one of the few taro landraces in Europe to carry protected EU geographical-indication status, prized for a dense, faintly nutty corm traditionally braised with pork and celery or simmered in olive oil and lemon. The large, triangular-ovate leaves thrive where soil stays consistently moist, and growers typically mound and irrigate heavily through the long warm season the corms need to size up. Plant divided corm offsets in deeply worked, humus-rich ground once the soil has warmed in spring, and keep plantings well watered, since the crop sulks and yields poorly under drought stress. Lift corms in autumn once the foliage begins to yellow and die back, curing them briefly before storage.
